procedure: Project the validated independent source contract from the immutable successor audit; retain its full source evidence, conventions and ambiguities in the sealed output.

payload.source_label: Sufficient smoothness of q and f(q) permits deriving (1.8) from the integral law (1.10)

contract.statement: For a one-dimensional, possibly vector-valued conservation law, suppose the time derivative of the integral of q between any two fixed spatial endpoints equals the flux at the left endpoint minus the flux at the right endpoint. If q and its composite flux f(q) are sufficiently smooth, then q_t + ∂_x[f(q)] = 0 follows. The source leaves the exact smoothness threshold unspecified and refers to Chapter 2 for the derivation. It explicitly warns that the classical differential equation does not hold at discontinuities, where the integral formulation remains fundamental. [Raw PDF p. 25, printed p. 3, (1.8); raw PDF p. 26, printed p. 4, (1.10) and Section 1.1.2 opening; raw PDF p. 27, printed p. 5, continuation of Section 1.1.2.]
assumptions: The integral conservation identity d/dt ∫[x₁,x₂] q(x,t) dx = f(q(x₁,t)) − f(q(x₂,t)) holds for any two spatial points x₁ and x₂. Its time dependence is understood over the times under consideration; no separate time interval is specified. [Raw PDF p. 26, printed p. 4, Section 1.1.1, (1.10) and its introduction.]

q and the composite flux f(q) are sufficiently smooth. The selected passage states this condition without prescribing a precise differentiability class. [Raw PDF p. 26, printed p. 4, Section 1.1.2, opening sentence.]

This is the one-dimensional conservation-law setting, including vector systems and nonlinear flux functions. [Raw PDF p. 25, printed p. 3, Section 1.1 opening; raw PDF p. 26, printed p. 4, opening paragraph.]

The displayed equations have no source term; the source explicitly distinguishes nonconserved quantities for which such terms must be added. [Raw PDF p. 26, printed p. 4, Section 1.1.1, contaminant discussion.]

Hyperbolic equations frame the chapter, but the selected derivation sentence does not impose a separate spectral condition on the flux Jacobian. The preceding discussion associates such conditions with hyperbolicity. [Raw PDF p. 25, printed p. 3, discussion after (1.9); raw PDF p. 26, printed p. 4, Section 1.1.2 opening.]

The smoothness proviso limits the classical differential formulation: the source warns that discontinuities can arise and that equation (1.8) does not hold classically at them. [Raw PDF pp. 26–27, printed pp. 4–5, Section 1.1.2.]
quantifiers: q is a state depending on one spatial coordinate x and time t, with inherited notation q : ℝ × ℝ → ℝᵐ; m is the number of state components. [Raw PDF p. 23, printed p. 1, notation following (1.1); raw PDF p. 26, printed p. 4, opening paragraph.]

f is the flux function of the state q; its values have the components needed for the vector conservation equation. The matching vector type is implicit in the displayed equations. [Raw PDF p. 25, printed p. 3, (1.8); raw PDF p. 26, printed p. 4, (1.10) and component interpretation.]

x₁ and x₂ are arbitrary spatial endpoints, held fixed in the displayed time derivative; x and t are the variables in the resulting PDE. Fixity of the endpoints is indicated structurally by their notation without time dependence. [Raw PDF p. 26, printed p. 4, sentence preceding (1.10) and (1.10); raw PDF p. 25, printed p. 3, (1.8).]
